quotes.quote: Africa: Rivers Nile, Niger, Senegal, Lake Chad Basin and Gambia basin.

sections.html:
• Common name: Nile auchenoglanis
  • IUCN Red List: Least Concern (IUCN 2020). The species has a wide distribution with no known major widespread threats.
Africa: Rivers Nile, Niger, Senegal, Lake Chad Basin and Gambia basin.
Commonly occurs in running water, lakes and submerged vegetation in the Sudd, rare in fringing vegetation.
Feeds on the bottom on mud, debris, insects, notably chironomid larvae and mollusks. (Geerinckx & Vreven 2013).

All Auchenoglanis can grow to a length of more than 40 cm, but as they feed mainly on small food particles they are usually very peaceful towards even much smaller tankmates. The meaty lips that serve for the detection of food in mud led to the nickname "kissing mouths" for Auchenoglanis in aquaristic circles.
Gravid fish are recorded throughout the year with a peak in the dry season.

Until recently only two species of Auchenoglanis were recognized as valid: A. biscutatus from the Nile and the whole of West Africa and A. occidentalis from Central Africa. But in 2010 the genus was revised by Retzer, who accepted a total of 8 different species, 7 already described formerly and one new species, namely A. senegali.

The species from the Niger, which is imported here, looks most similar to A. wittei from the Congo, but according to Retzer the Auchenoglanis from the Niger belongs most probably to a still scientifically undescribed species. For these reasons the fish is listed as Auchenoglanis biscutatus.

The main description for A. biscutatus is that the body and adipose fin in adults is either light brown or grey with small, distinct spots on the rayed fins that do not form bands. The shape of the nuchal plate is also distinctive from all other congeners in the genus. The species depicted in the first thumbnail image was originally thought to be a juvenile of A. occidentalis.

A. biscutatus is distinguished from A. occidentalis by a postorbital head length that is greater than the preorbital head length, an adipose fin that rises abruptly, and a maxillary barbel with a tip not darker than the head colour.

Teugels et al. (1991) considered the genus Auchenoglanis to be comprised of two valid species: A. biscutatus and A. occidentalis. Following work by Michael Retzer (2010) there were 8 species in the genus: A. acuticeps (now considered a synonym of A. occidentalis), A. biscutatus, A. occidentalis, A. sacchii, A. senegali (now considered a synonym of A. biscutatus), A. tanganicanus, A. tchadiensis and A. wittei. A later re-evaluation based on biometric, meristic and other morphological data reconfirmed only two valid species within the genus. A. occidentalis has a very large distribution, from Senegal to Tanzania.

Etymology: the genus name Auchenoglanis is a replacement name for Auchenaspis Bleeker 1858 (preoccupied in fossil fishes); auchenos, neck, and aspis, shield, refer to the broad nuchal shield; glanis, sheatfish (Silurus glanis), is now used as a general term for catfish. The specific name biscutatus: bi-, two; scutatus, shielded, referring to the nuchal shield divided into two parts.
